selection_principle: Deliberate range, not top-scores: fixed life-stage quotas; mix of famous/obscure, funny/emotional/action/philosophical/devotional/friendship; roles: child, king/statesman, adviser/teacher; includes morally complex and tone-sensitive pieces to calibrate the editorial voice.

stories.reason: The opening prophecy — establishes Kamsa, the doom, and the stakes for the whole biography. Famous, dramatic, sets the series tone.
The midnight birth in the prison cell — the most iconic image of the entire tradition.
The night crossing of the Yamuna with the newborn — wonder and protective love; classic visual.
Kamsa comes to kill the newborn girl and the illusion slips away — dramatic reversal; tests the devotional voice.
Putana, the demon nurse — eerie, famous, and the first of the childhood demons; establishes Gokul.
Trinavarta the whirlwind — pure childhood action with a twist (the child heavier than the world).
Butter-stealing — the funniest and most human story in the corpus; calibrates humour in the voice.
Krishna eats mud and shows the universe in his mouth — the cosmos-in-a-mouthbeat; philosophical wonder.
The mortar and the twin trees (the name 'Damodara') — famous, combines mischief with liberation.
Garga names the boys in secret — warm, ceremonial, explains the names; rarely told.
The dance on Kaliya's hoods — the most famous Vrindavan image after Govardhan; action + surrender.
Krishna lifts Govardhan Hill — the central statement of the childhood; test of the peak-and-resolution structure.
The rasa dance — the most delicate story in the corpus; requires the devotional-but-not-preachy voice at its best.
The gopis leave their homes to follow Krishna — emotional counterpart to the rasa; separation and love.
Krishna swallows the wildfire to save the herd — pure wonder, a visual feast, less famous than Kaliya/Govardhan.
Aghasura — the giant serpent-demon and the friends' rescue; eerie and heroic at once.
After Brahma hides the calves, Krishna becomes all the calves and boys — philosophical multiplication; a subtle classic.
Akrura sees the divine vision in the Yamuna on the way to Mathura — mystical; bridges Vrindavan to Mathura.
The slaying of Kamsa — the first great climax of the biography; ends the childhood half.
The wrestling match with Mushtika and Chanura — arena action; the crowd, the kings, the arena.
Kubja the hunchback — Krishna's kindness and a flash of wit; a small, human story.
Retrieving the preceptor's son from the underworld — adventure, a compact quest with gods and sea.
Krishna carries off Rukmini — the great romance; also the model for the 'message' story.
The Syamantaka jewel: accusation, the bear-king, the wrestling match — mystery and vindication.
Narakasura's slaying and the rescue of the princesses — a Dwaraka classic; big action set-piece.
Krishna eats Sudama's flat rice — the friendship story; tests restraint and tenderness.
The brahmana's sons restored — an obscure mystery-adventure with a cosmic tour; proof the index holds treasures.
Viswakarma builds Dwaraka — Krishna as statesman and city-builder; the founding of the sea-city.
Paundraka, the false Vasudeva — a striking identity story (a king who claims to BE Krishna); obscure.
Draupadi's endless robes — the most famous miracle of protection; emotional and iconic.
The burning of Khandava — Krishna and Arjuna vs Indra; epic action and the gift of the forest.
The slaying of Shishupala at the Rajasuya — court drama, the hundred-offences prophecy, the discus.
Krishna receives the first honour at the Rajasuya — statesmanship, ritual, and the seeds of Shishupala's rage.
Krishna counsels Arjuna to abduct Subhadra — the matchmaker; light, funny, and warm.
The Durvasa test — Krishna eats one grain and the sage's hunger is satisfied; clever and quietly funny.
Arjuna's despair before the war — the emotional opening of the Gita; the human entry into the teaching.
The Vishvarupa — the cosmic form; the philosophical peak of the corpus; a vision story.
Krishna reveals Karna's birth and offers him the kingdom — identity, loyalty, and heartbreak.
Krishna sinks the chariot to save Arjuna from Karna's dart — the charioteer's loyalty made literal.
The Ashvatthama stratagem — Krishna's most morally contested decision; the adviser under pressure.
Krishna urges Arjuna to slay the distressed Karna — the hardest moral test in the corpus; essential for editorial calibration.
Gandhari's curse — Krishna accepts it with a smile; grief, anger, and grace at the war's end.
The Yadava fratricide at Prabhasa — the tragedy of the house; the turning point of the end.
The hunter Jara's arrow — the tender, strange ending of the earthly life; the final image.
Bhrigu tests the three gods — a philosophical fable about where greatness truly lives; obscure and sharp.
Pingala the courtesan's renunciation — an Uddhava parable of letting go; unusual and moving.
The pigeon and the hunter's net — a parable of love and loss; the most poignant of the Uddhava tales.
King Nriga freed from a lizard's body — a bizarre, moral fable in the middle of Dwaraka; very rarely told.
